passage: In Marseille, Leila and her cousin Layla were given a school project: reduce your family's carbon footprint for a month. Leila rolled her eyes. "One family won't save the planet." Layla, who had read more, explained that most warming came from burning coal, oil and gas for power and transport. "So small things add up if lots of people do them. And we can push the school too." They made a list: walk or cycle to school, turn off lights, eat fewer takeaway meals in plastic. Leila's father grumbled about the bus. At the end of the month, their class wrote to the town council asking for a safer bike lane. Leila was surprised how good it felt to sign her name.

qa.q: What did the cousins' class write to the town council about?
qa.a: They asked for a safer bike lane.

qa.q: How did Leila feel at the start of the project, and how did that change?
qa.a: She was doubtful and dismissive, rolling her eyes, but by the end she felt surprised and good about taking part.

qa.q: What made the cousins' approach realistic?
qa.a: They picked small personal steps and also joined a group action, the letter to the council, which could make a bigger difference.

qa.q: How might Leila's father see the changes?
qa.a: He grumbled about the bus, suggesting he found them inconvenient, but he might come round if he sees the girls' effort.

grounding: It shows teens learning the causes of climate change and taking realistic personal and group action.

passage: The school's eco-club in Pune had a new project: cut the canteen's waste. Vaibhav, Class 10, thought it would be boring. His friend Bhupen had checked how much food was thrown away each day and brought a photo of the overflowing bins. "That's rotting food making methane," Bhupen said. "It warms the planet more than we think." Vaibhav looked at the photo for a long time. They met the canteen manager, who was worried about losing money. Bhupen suggested smaller portions with free refills. The manager agreed to try it for two weeks. The bins got lighter. Vaibhav started a compost pit behind the science lab. He didn't like getting his hands dirty, but he liked the numbers going down.

qa.q: What did Bhupen say rotting food makes?
qa.a: He said it makes methane.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav look at the photo for a long time?
qa.a: Seeing the overflowing bins made the problem feel real and changed his view that the project would be boring.

qa.q: What made Bhupen's suggestion to the canteen manager workable?
qa.a: Smaller portions with free refills addressed the manager's worry about money while cutting waste.

qa.q: How might the canteen manager see the project after two weeks?
qa.a: He might be pleased to see less waste and no loss, and more open to the students' next idea.

grounding: It shows teens understanding a cause of climate change and taking practical group action at school.

passage:
Dear Eshaan,
You asked me why I've stopped asking Papa to drive me to tuition. Honestly, it's the climate project we did in school. I learned that cars burning petrol are one of the big reasons the earth is heating up. At first I felt scared and hopeless. What can I even do? But our teacher said we can't fix it alone, but we can do our part and push for bigger changes.
So now I cycle to tuition, I carry a steel bottle, and our class is asking the principal for solar lights on the terrace.
I know you think it's too small. Maybe it is. But it feels better than doing nothing. 🙂 Come cycling with me on Sunday?
Vinita

qa.q: What is Vinita's class asking the principal for?
qa.a: They are asking for solar lights on the terrace.

qa.q: How did Vinita feel when first learning about climate change?
qa.a: Vinita felt scared and hopeless, unsure what one person could do.

qa.q: Why is Vinita's mix of actions a sensible response?
qa.a: Vinita takes small personal steps like cycling and also joins a group request, which is realistic without being overwhelming.

qa.q: If you were Eshaan, how might you respond to Vinita's invitation?
qa.a: You might still think it's small, but joining Vinita for a cycle ride could be a fun first step.

grounding: A teen's letter explains the causes of climate change the writer learned and the realistic actions they are taking.

passage: So, you asked why I started the climate club. Honestly, it began with panic. I'm Reena, sixteen. I'd watch videos about melting ice and feel so helpless I couldn't sleep. My friend Yusuf said, 'Panicking doesn't cool anything.' So we learned the basics properly. Burning coal, petrol and gas puts gases in the air that trap heat, like a blanket that keeps getting thicker. Okay. Then we asked: what can a school actually do? We counted fans and lights left on in empty classrooms; it was shocking. We got a monitor in each class to switch them off. We started a carpool list for parents. It's small. It won't save the planet alone. But I sleep better when I'm doing something real.

qa.q: What did Reena and Yusuf count in empty classrooms?
qa.a: Fans and lights left on.

qa.q: How did Reena feel before starting the climate club?
qa.a: Reena felt helpless and panicked, so much that sleep wouldn't come after climate videos.

qa.q: What made the club's actions realistic?
qa.a: They chose practical steps within the school's control, like classroom monitors for lights and a carpool list.

qa.q: How might Yusuf see Reena's change from panic to action?
qa.a: Yusuf would likely feel that the blunt comment helped turn Reena's worry into something useful.

grounding: A teen explains learning the causes of climate change and taking realistic group action.

passage: I'm Nirmala, and I teach science at the school in Gangtok. This year I watched Tenzin, fifteen, become quietly obsessed. It started after his grandfather said the snow on the far peaks came later and left earlier than in his youth. Tenzin asked me for old weather records. He spent lunch breaks in the library copying numbers from district reports. Then he organised a Saturday group to survey trees along the stream, noting which ones were flowering early. I never heard him say he was worried, but he rarely smiled during the survey. At the end of term he presented a simple chart and a plan: a school rain-water tank and a no-plastic canteen. Six students signed up. I don't know how he feels about the future. He keeps working.

qa.q: What did Tenzin's grandfather say about the snow?
qa.a: That it came later and left earlier than in his youth.

qa.q: What does Tenzin rarely smiling during the survey suggest, according to Nirmala?
qa.a: It suggests he may have been concerned or serious about the changes, though Nirmala can't be sure.

qa.q: What made Tenzin's approach more than just worry?
qa.a: He gathered real records, surveyed local trees and turned findings into practical school actions.

qa.q: How might Tenzin's grandfather feel seeing the chart?
qa.a: He might feel proud that his memory inspired real study and action. 🙂

grounding: An observer describes a teen learning climate evidence locally and leading realistic small actions.

passage:
Monday. In geography, Uday copied "burning coal, petrol and gas traps heat" into his notebook and felt nothing; it was one more exam line. That evening the power went out again in the heatwave, and he lay sweating, scrolling videos of melting glaciers until he felt sick and useless.
Two weeks later. Santosh, tired of the same gloomy talk, said, "Stop doom-scrolling. What do we actually control?" They made a list on the back of a maths sheet: the scooter rides to school, the classroom fans left running, the canteen's plastic cups.
A month later. Eight students now cycled together on Wednesdays, and the prefects checked fans at every break. Uday knew it wouldn't cool the planet. But when he explained to his little sister why the air was getting hotter, he could say it without the sick feeling.

qa.q: How many students cycled together on Wednesdays a month later?
qa.a: Eight students.

qa.q: How did Uday's feelings change between the first night and a month later?
qa.a: At first Uday felt sick and useless from doom-scrolling; a month later, after small group actions, he could talk about it calmly instead of feeling hopeless.

qa.q: What made Santosh's question useful, and what could the group try next?
qa.a: It moved them from worry to what they actually control; next they could track results, like fans switched off, and share them with the school.

qa.q: How might Uday's little sister experience his explanation?
qa.a: She would probably find it easier to understand and less frightening, because Uday explains it calmly instead of passing on panic.

grounding: Over a month, a teenager moves from exam-line knowledge and climate dread to understanding and small group action.

passage: Aditi, sit, your tea will go cold. You ask why your Kalyani Paati still carries this cloth bag everywhere. Blame Mohan. Twenty years ago I taught science in Belagavi, and Mohan was the boy who argued with everything. One day he stood up and said, "Ma'am, if cars and factories are warming the earth, what can a schoolboy do? Nothing." The class laughed. I had no answer ready. That week he came back with a notebook: how many plastic bags his family used, how many scooter trips his father took that could be walked. "Not nothing," he said. "Small." He got the whole class counting. The shopkeeper near school started keeping cloth bags because thirty children kept asking. So that is how I learned it, from a boy of fifteen: knowing why it happens is half the work, and choosing what you can really do is the other half.

qa.q: What did Mohan record in his notebook?
qa.a: How many plastic bags his family used and how many scooter trips his father took that could be walked.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel when the class laughed and there was no answer ready?
qa.a: Kalyani seems to have felt unsure and a little embarrassed as the teacher, which is why Mohan's notebook left such a strong mark.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Mohan's thinking, and why did it work?
qa.a: Mohan moved from 'nothing' to counting his own family's bags and trips; measuring made the problem concrete and gave the class realistic actions.

qa.q: How might the shopkeeper near the school have seen the children's requests?
qa.a: The shopkeeper probably saw real demand, with thirty children asking, and found cloth bags worth stocking, showing how small actions spread.

grounding: A grandmother tells how a fifteen-year-old student turned climate helplessness into small measurable actions.

passage: Rekha had planned a slide show. Then, on Thursday evening, the vice-principal moved the eco-club assembly to Friday morning, and the projector in the hall was still broken. Naveen stared at the laptop. "Twelve slides of graphs. Useless." Rekha pulled out the chart paper left over from Diwali decorations. "We only need three things. Why it's getting hotter. What our school wastes. What we'll do." They worked on the floor of her room until midnight: a sun over a grey blanket of smoke for the greenhouse effect, a tally of forty lights found on in empty classrooms, and a sign-up sheet for "Switch-Off Monitors". In the morning her hands shook holding the chart. But thirty-one names were on the sheet by lunch, and a Class 6 boy asked to be monitor for the whole corridor.

qa.q: How many lights did the tally show on in empty classrooms?
qa.a: Forty lights.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling as she held the chart in the morning?
qa.a: Rekha felt nervous, with shaking hands after the rushed night, but went ahead anyway.

qa.q: How did the group handle the broken projector, and why did it still work?
qa.a: They cut twelve slides down to three simple ideas on chart paper, which kept the message clear and ended with an action students could join.

qa.q: How might Naveen feel when thirty-one names appear on the sheet?
qa.a: Naveen, who thought the plan was useless without slides, would probably feel relieved and proud that the simpler version worked.

grounding: Under time pressure, a teenager explains climate causes simply and launches a realistic school energy action.

passage:
In May, the Delhi heatwave closed Yogesh's school for a week. The water tanks ran dry in their colony.
Yogesh read about how cities trap heat: concrete, few trees, many ACs pushing heat outside.
He talked to Irawati, who lived on the third floor. "What if we plant trees on the empty strip by the park, and paint our terraces white?"
"Will that stop climate change?"
"No. But it'll make our colony cooler, and it's something."
They got fifteen families to join. The RWA gave permission for twelve saplings. By the monsoon, the saplings were knee-high.
Irawati said, "We should tell the next colony."
Yogesh grinned. "Already made a poster."

qa.q: How many saplings did the RWA give permission for?
qa.a: Twelve saplings.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when he said "it's something"?
qa.a: Yogesh felt realistic but hopeful, wanting to act even though it couldn't fix everything.

qa.q: Why is Yogesh's plan a realistic climate action?
qa.a: It tackles local heat with trees and white terraces and brings in neighbours, rather than promising to solve everything.

qa.q: How does Irawati see the project by the end?
qa.a: Irawati is convinced enough to want other colonies to do it too.

grounding: A teen links urban heat to climate causes and organises a realistic local action.

passage:
"Why bother?" said Naveen. "One person can't change the climate."
Lakshmi put down her cycle. "One person, no. But it's not just one."
"Factories and power plants make most of the emissions."
"Right. That's why we need rules for them too. That's voting and pressure. But small things add up, and they change what's normal."
"Like what?"
"Like cycling to school. Our class did it for a month. Twenty of us. The principal's now building a cycle stand."
Naveen thought. "So you did one thing, and it made a bigger thing."
"Exactly."
"I'll cycle tomorrow if you ride with me."
"Deal."

qa.q: What is the principal now building?
qa.a: A cycle stand.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when he said "Why bother?"?
qa.a: Naveen felt doubtful and discouraged about individual action.

qa.q: What argument did Lakshmi use to change Naveen's mind?
qa.a: She agreed big emitters need rules, but showed how small group actions add up and change norms, like the cycle stand.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel when Naveen agrees to cycle?
qa.a: Lakshmi probably feels pleased 🙂 that her example persuaded him.

grounding: Two teens discuss the causes of climate change and the value of small actions.

passage:
Two years ago, the river near our town flooded. Water came into our ground floor. We lost my school books and Maa's sewing machine.
I'm Pankaj. After the flood, I got angry and started reading. I learnt that warmer air holds more moisture, so rains can get heavier. I learnt about burning fuel and cutting forests.
But reading made me feel helpless. Then my friend Gargi said, "Let's do something small." We started a Sunday cycle group to reduce short scooter trips. Then we planted bamboo along the river bank with the forest department.
It won't stop floods. But I feel less helpless. And forty people cycle with us now.

qa.q: What did the flood destroy?
qa.a: Pankaj's school books and Maa's sewing machine.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling after reading about climate change?
qa.a: Pankaj felt angry and then helpless about the size of the problem.

qa.q: What helped Pankaj move from helplessness to action?
qa.a: Gargi's suggestion to do something small, which led to a cycle group and bamboo planting.

qa.q: How might Gargi see the group's growth to forty people?
qa.a: Gargi likely feels proud and encouraged that their small idea grew.

grounding: A young person recalls learning climate causes after a flood and starting realistic group action.

passage:
Teacher's note. Kavitha, geography, Eco Club supervisor.
Urmila came to the Eco Club overwhelmed after a news report on melting glaciers. "What's the point? We're just kids."
I asked her to first explain the cause to the club: burning coal, petrol and diesel releases gases that trap heat, like a blanket that keeps getting thicker. She did, with a chart. That seemed to calm her.
Then I asked, "What's one thing our school burns fuel for?" The club listed: generator, school buses, parents' cars at pick-up.
Urmila proposed a "walk or cycle Wednesday" for students within two kilometres and a check of how long the generator runs. She surveyed the classes herself.
Results after a month: forty students joining Wednesdays. It's not saving the world, as she said. But she's stopped saying "what's the point".

qa.q: What did the Eco Club list that the school burns fuel for?
qa.a: The generator, school buses and parents' cars at pick-up.

qa.q: How was Urmila feeling when she came to the club?
qa.a: Urmila felt overwhelmed and hopeless after the news report on melting glaciers.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha's approach help Urmila?
qa.a: Understanding the cause first calmed her, and finding one local, realistic action turned hopelessness into something she could do.

qa.q: How might the forty students on Wednesdays see Urmila's idea?
qa.a: They might enjoy it and feel part of something useful, even if it's small.

grounding: Shows a teen learning the causes of climate change and organising a realistic group action at school.

passage:
Wednesday
Diary, Aparna here. It was 45 degrees today. School cut the afternoon classes. Ira and I walked home under one umbrella and still felt like we were melting.
I asked her, "Is this climate change or just summer?" She said her science teacher said both: summer is normal, but heatwaves are getting longer and more often because the planet is warming from all the fuel we burn.
I felt panicky, then angry, then tired.
Then Ira said her building has twelve kids going to our school, all in separate cars. "What if we just shared?"
So we made a list tonight. Four cars instead of twelve on most days. We asked our parents; they're calling each other now.
It's a tiny thing. I know it doesn't fix the heat. But I'm less panicky when I'm doing something.

qa.q: How many cars do the kids in Ira's building plan to use on most days?
qa.a: Four cars instead of twelve.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel after Ira explained heatwaves?
qa.a: Aparna felt panicky, then angry, then tired, and later less panicky once they started doing something.

qa.q: Why is the car-sharing plan a realistic action?
qa.a: It's small, local and involves parents, so it can actually happen and cut fuel use, even if it doesn't fix everything.

qa.q: How might the parents in the building see the teens' list?
qa.a: The parents may feel impressed and willing to help, since the plan also saves them time and trips.

grounding: Illustrates a teen understanding a cause of heatwaves and taking a realistic small group action.

passage: The pond behind the Shiv temple in Gargi's village had shrunk to a cracked brown circle by April. Her grandfather said it never used to dry before the monsoon. In science class that week, Gargi learned how burning coal and diesel traps heat, and how hotter summers pull water out of ponds and soil faster. She walked home with Yusuf, whose father ran the diesel pump for the fields. "So we stop the pump?" Yusuf asked, half joking. "No," Gargi said. "But we can do something small that's real." They went to their teacher, and the eco club set up a rooftop rain barrel at school, then a sign-up sheet for households wanting help with their own. Only six families signed up. Gargi pinned the list on the panchayat notice board anyway.

qa.q: What did the eco club set up at the school?
qa.a: The eco club set up a rooftop rain barrel.

qa.q: How might Gargi have felt when only six families signed up?
qa.a: She was probably disappointed, yet still determined, since she pinned the list on the panchayat notice board anyway.

qa.q: Why was Gargi's answer to Yusuf a wise one?
qa.a: Instead of an impossible fix like stopping the pump, she chose a small, practical step the school and some families could actually take.

qa.q: How might Yusuf feel about the talk of diesel and heat, given his father's job?
qa.a: Yusuf might feel a bit defensive or uneasy, which may be why he half-joked about stopping the pump.

grounding: Shows a teen linking the causes of warming to her village's drying pond and choosing a realistic group action.
